Text 1: Vaccinology and its sceptics
Around the world, vaccines are in retreat, shunned by populations who, for the most part, have never been exposed to the diseases that blighted or shortened the lives of their grandparents’ generation. But with the possible exception of quinine – for centuries the only treatment for malaria – and antibiotics, vaccines have saved more lives than any other intervention in medical history. This growing vaccine hesitancy is not confined to a particular religious or ethnic group or bounded by ideology, class or economic circumstance. Wealthy parents are as likely to believe the hype surrounding the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) and its link to autism as poorer parents.
Meanwhile, diseases once virtually eradicated in developed nations have come back with a vengeance. 2018 saw nearly 83,000 cases of measles across Europe, for example – triple the 2017 number. Little wonder the World Health Organisation (WHO) has described vaccine hesitancy as one of the top ten threats the world faces in coming years. So why is this? Ben Foley of the Vaccine Institute, Florida, says that “although it’s difficult to gauge the impact of social media, the suspicion is that it has skewed the game heavily in favour of so-called “anti-vaxxers or anti-vaccination campaigners.” An example of this is an investigation which found that the top 12 Facebook groups returned by a search for “vaccination” were all anti-vaccine. “Some, like the Vaccination Re-education Discussion Forum and NVIC are very easy to spot as anti-vaxxers,” he adds. His comments have certainly ruffled some feathers. Janice Armstrong, a founding member of the National Vaccine Information Centre (NVIC) insists “our mission is only to promote informed consent, by offering neutral, evidence-based information about vaccines,” but as Ben Foley points out, “its website has many stories about vaccine-damaged children and the “harassment” of parents for making “informed vaccine choices,” which to me is inconsistent with neutrality.”
Faced with online propaganda, the response of public health officials has been to double down on positive vaccine messages. Associate Professor of Immunotherapeutics and Vaccinology, Rachael Jenkins, of Boston University says “the problem with this strategy is that it sidesteps an uncomfortable truth about vaccine science: namely, that there is a lot that vaccinologists still don’t know about vaccines and their interaction with our immune systems. It also fails to address the rare cases where vaccines fail and are dangerous.” A good example of this is GlaxoSmithKline’s Pandemrix vaccine, which was rolled out across Europe during the 2009 swine flu pandemic, only to be withdrawn when it was found that it was associated with a 14-fold increase in the risk of narcolepsy in children. Although the study was published in the British Medical Journal, few journalists covered the story, it is speculated, for fear of being accused of fuelling vaccine hesitancy.
Medical researchers have also faced startling pushback from colleagues for daring to question the effectiveness of flu vaccines. This is despite the fact that, even in a good year, these vaccines are at best 60% effective, and in some years, such as the 2004-5 flu season, their efficacy can be as low as 10%. In fact, a 2018 meta-analysis by the Cochrane collaboration found that, on average, you would need to vaccinate 71 healthy people to prevent a single case of flu. One reason for this is the difficulty of matching the viruses used in flu vaccines with the dominant virus strains that emerge during the northern hemisphere winter. Another is that the technology for manufacturing flu vaccines is very old and still imperfectly understood. Most flu vaccines are made by cultivating the influenza virus in chick eggs, a technology that dates to the 1930s. The egg-adapted virus is then purified and inactivated, before being produced in bulk – a task that takes about six months.
To those who may dislike the jab of a needle in their arm or have read on the internet that the flu vaccination program can make you “sicker than the disease”, such statistics may not inspire a great deal of confidence. But what if next year’s flu turned out to be a major killer, like the so-called Spanish influenza pandemic that swept the globe in 1918-19? On that occasion, there were no vaccines or antibiotics, and more than 50 million people died. Shouldn’t technology that could reduce a catastrophe on that scale, even marginally, be welcomed, not deprecated?
So rather than playing into the hands of anti-vaxxers, wouldn’t it be better for vaccine scientists to show a little humility and admit the gaps in their knowledge? Doing so need not detract from the message that vaccines such as MMR prevent thousands of measles deaths around the globe annually, or that the oral polio vaccine means that parents across the globe need no longer fear that their children will grow up crippled. In admitting that vaccines are sometimes associated with harm but pointing out that the benefits outweigh the risks, scientists stand to regain the trust of those who have become easy prey for the pseudo-scientific claims of anti-vaxxers. To admit that vaccinology is an imperfect science is not a sign of weakness, but of strength. Think of it as an inoculation against ignorance.
